_about: Dated events for the Read tab's "World around it", per parsha. Each parsha's events are chosen to fall inside its own window (see parshaDates.json): around the traditional date and inside the period scholars use. "note" says how uncertain the parsha's own date is. "approx" true means the year is shown with "c."; "endBCE" makes it a span. Parshiot not listed fall back to the era list in timeline.json.

lech-lecha.note: No one can date Abram. These events fall around the traditional date, c. 1738 BCE, and inside the Middle Bronze Age (c. 2000–1550 BCE), where scholars who try to date him usually place him. They show the world of that time; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: Egypt's 13th Dynasty takes over from the 12th and rules for about 150 years, until c. 1649 BCE.
events.significance: The traditional date of Abram's stay in Egypt (Genesis 12:10–20) falls in this dynasty. The Torah does not name the Pharaoh.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Thirteenth Dynasty of Egypt" (c. 1802–1649 BC)

events.description: Hammurabi becomes king of Babylon and reigns until c. 1750 BCE.
events.significance: Late in his reign he brings Mesopotamia under Babylon's rule. Abram's family came from Ur and Haran, in Mesopotamia (Genesis 11:31).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Hammurabi" (reign c. 1792–c. 1750 BC; "succeeded in uniting all of Mesopotamia")
Genesis 11:31; P. K. McCarter Jr. and R. S. Hendel, "The Patriarchal Age" (Ur "in southern Mesopotamia", Haran "in northwestern Mesopotamia")

events.description: Hammurabi defeats Zimri-Lim, king of Mari on the Euphrates, and razes the city about two years later.
events.significance: Mari's palace archive, over 25,000 tablets from about 1800–1750 BCE, is a major record of the Amorite kingdoms of Syria and Mesopotamia in this age.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mari, Syria" (Babylon invades c. 1761 BC; city razed after revolt c. 1759 BC; over 25,000 tablets, c. 1800–1750 BC)

events.description: Hammurabi's laws are set down near the end of his reign.
events.significance: Law 146 deals with a wife who gives her husband a slave woman, who bears him children and then claims equal standing with her mistress, much as Hagar looks down on Sarai (Genesis 16:4).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Code of Hammurabi" (composed c. 1753 BC)
The Code of Hammurabi, tr. L. W. King, laws 144–147 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
Genesis 16:4

vayikra.note: Tradition dates the Tabernacle, where these laws are given, to c. 1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1321 to 1185 BCE, across both.

events.description: Hittite king Mursili II prays for an end to a plague that has lasted twenty years, confessing that the Hittites broke an oath sworn to their storm-god.
events.significance: He pairs admitting the wrong with offerings. Leviticus 5 also joins confession (5:5) to an offering.

sources.title: "The Plague Prayer of Mursilis II", Early Indo-European Online, University of Texas at Austin (c. 1321–1295; broken oath; confession and offerings)
Eva von Dassow, "Contagion and Recovery in the Hittite Empire", History News Network ("the twentieth year")
Leviticus 5:5

events.description: Battle of Kadesh: Ramesses II of Egypt fights the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria.
events.significance: About 15 years later Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III make the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Battle of Kadesh" (generally dated to May 1274 BCE; treaty some 15 years later)
Wikipedia, "Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty" (around 1259 BC; "the oldest known surviving peace treaty")

events.description: Pharaoh Merneptah's victory stele says “Israel is laid waste—its seed is no more.”
events.significance: The earliest certain mention of Israel outside the Bible; an older reading on a statue base in Berlin is debated. It names Israel as a people, alongside places in Canaan.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Merneptah Stele" (year 5 of Merneptah, c. 1208 BCE)
Wikipedia, "Berlin pedestal relief" (Manfred Görg: it "may have originally contained" an older reference to Israel)

events.description: Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, is destroyed. Its ritual texts, written before the destruction, list offerings including the šlmm, the “peace-offering”.
events.significance: The word matches Hebrew shelamim, the well-being offering in Leviticus 3. The texts list what was offered more than they explain what the rites meant.

sources.title: Dennis Pardee, Ritual and Cult at Ugarit (Society of Biblical Literature, 2002): destruction "ca. 1185 B.C.E."; šlmm "peace-offering", "cognate with Hebrew šəlāmîm"

shemot.note: Tradition dates Moses at the burning bush to c. 1314 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1319 to 1275 BCE, across both.

events.description: Horemheb, commander of Egypt's army, becomes king. He names his vizier Paramessu as his heir, who becomes Ramesses I, founder of the 19th Dynasty.
events.significance: Shemot's story of oppression begins with “a new king over Egypt” (Exodus 1:8). The Torah does not name him.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled "between 1319 BC and 1292 BC"; authored the Edict of Horemheb)
Wikipedia, "Ramesses I" (Horemheb's vizier; "founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt's 19th Dynasty")
Exodus 1:8

events.description: Ramesses II becomes king and builds Pi-Ramesses, a new capital in the eastern Nile Delta. The site had been a summer palace under his father, Seti I.
events.significance: Exodus 1:11 names Raamses as a city Israel was forced to build. Many scholars identify it with Pi-Ramesses; others see the name as reflecting a later age.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Pi-Ramesses" ("new capital built by ... Ramesses II (1279–1213 BC)"; summer palace under Seti I; identified with biblical Raamses, though some see an anachronism)
Exodus 1:11

events.description: A taskmaster's leather roll records daily brick quotas for workmen. One entry: a target of 2,000 bricks, 1,630 delivered, 370 short.
events.significance: In Shemot, Pharaoh keeps Israel's quota of bricks unchanged while taking away their straw (Exodus 5:7–8).

sources.title: Manfred Bietak and Gary A. Rendsburg, "Egypt and the Exodus," in Ancient Israel, ed. H. Shanks (Biblical Archaeology Society): the Louvre Leather Roll, "dated to year 5 of Ramesses II"; "(target) 2,000 bricks ... total 1,630 / deficit 370"
Exodus 5:7-8

vaera.note: Tradition dates the plagues to c. 1314–1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1329 to 1213 BCE, across both.

events.description: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela announces the end of Akhenaten's Aten religion and the reopening of the temples of Egypt's old gods.
events.significance: In Egypt, royal power and the gods' temples went together. In Vaera, Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh and his magicians (Exodus 7:10–12).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Restoration Stela" (repeals Atenism and reinstates "the original, indigenous religion of ancient Egypt"; Aidan Dodson dates it to "Year 4")
Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (ruled c. 1332–1323 BC)
Exodus 7:10-12

events.description: Egyptian lists of enemy lands, copied at Amara in Nubia under Seti I or Ramesses II, name “the land of the Shasu yhw”, a group of nomads.
events.significance: In Vaera, God tells Moses the patriarchs did not know Him by the name YHWH (Exodus 6:3). Scholars debate whether this place-name is connected to that name.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Shasu" (13th-century copies "ordered by Seti I or by Ramesses II at Amara" list Shasu "of yhw"; Astour: it "corresponds very precisely to the Hebrew Tetragrammaton")
Exodus 6:3

events.description: Ramesses II takes the throne, probably on 31 May 1279 BCE. He will reign 66 years, the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh.
events.significance: Most scholars who accept a historical core to the Exodus place it in the 13th century, in his reign. The Torah does not name the pharaoh.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Ramesses II" (accession "most Egyptologists believe to be 31 May 1279 BC"; "66-year rule was also the longest recorded reign of any pharaoh")
Wikipedia, "The Exodus" (most scholars who accept a historical core date it "to the thirteenth century BCE at the time of Ramses II")

bo.note: Tradition dates the Exodus to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1322 to 1244 BCE, across both.

events.description: Hittite king Šuppiluliuma I dies. A plague, brought to his land by prisoners taken from Egypt's army, ravages the Hittites for about twenty years.
events.significance: The plague probably also killed his heir, Arnuwanda I. His son Mursili II later prays for it to end.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Šuppiluliuma I" (died c. 1322 BC; captives caused "an outbreak of plague that ravaged Hittite society for at least two decades"; often considered the cause of his and Arnuwanda I's deaths)
Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (the plague prayers)

events.description: Hittite king Mursili II's annals say that as he set out on campaign, “the Sun gave a sign”. Most scholars identify it with the solar eclipse of 24 June 1312 BCE.
events.significance: This is not the Torah's darkness, which lasts three days (Exodus 10:22). It shows how kings of the time read the sky for signs.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mursili's eclipse" ("the Sun gave a sign"; "now more commonly identified as the one of 24 June 1312 BC")
Wikipedia, "Mursili II" ("most scholars accept the 1312 BC event"; alternative 13 April 1308 BC)
Exodus 10:22

events.description: Ramesses II builds the rock temples of Abu Simbel in Nubia over about twenty years. The great temple honours Amun, Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and the deified king himself.
events.significance: In Bo, God declares judgment “on all the gods of Egypt” (Exodus 12:12). At Abu Simbel, the pharaoh sits among those gods.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Abu Simbel" (construction "started in c. 1264 BC" and lasted "until 1244 BC"; dedicated to Amun, Ra-Horakhty, Ptah "as well as to the deified Ramesses himself")
Exodus 12:12

beshalach.note: Tradition dates the crossing of the sea to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1323 to 1200 BCE, across both.

events.description: Tutankhamun dies at about 18. His tomb holds a painted chest with battle scenes and a gold-leaf picture of him shooting arrows from a chariot.
events.significance: In Beshalach, Pharaoh chases Israel with “six hundred chosen chariots” (Exodus 14:7).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (c. 1342 – c. 1323 BC; "battle depictions on the painted treasure chest in his tomb, and a gold leaf picture of him during chariot archery")
Exodus 14:7

events.description: In his first year, Seti I marches along the Ways of Horus, a chain of forts with wells across northern Sinai from Egypt to Gaza, fighting Shasu nomads on the way.
events.significance: Beshalach says God did not lead Israel “by way of the land of the Philistines”, the coast road, lest they turn back at the sight of war (Exodus 13:17).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruled 1290–1279 BC; "In his first regnal year" he led his armies along the Horus road, "a series of military forts, each with a well"; fought the Shasu)
Wikipedia, "Via Maris" (Egyptian "Way of Horus"; also called "Way of the Philistines")
Exodus 13:17

events.description: An Egyptian frontier officer reports chasing two runaway slaves past the fort of Tjeku and the Migdol of Seti Merneptah, and asks how many men are pursuing them.
events.significance: Exodus 14:2–9 also has Migdol and a pursuit of escaped slaves. Manfred Bietak and Gary Rendsburg compare the two.

sources.title: Manfred Bietak and Gary A. Rendsburg, "Egypt and the Exodus," in Ancient Israel, ed. H. Shanks (Biblical Archaeology Society): P. Anastasi V, "dated to the reign of Seti II"; "two slaves have escaped Egypt into the desert"; Tjeku, Migdol
Center for Online Judaic Studies, "Papyrus Anastasi V, c. 1200 BCE" ("This surely does not confirm the Israelite Exodus")
Exodus 14:2-9

yitro.note: Tradition dates the giving of the Torah at Sinai to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1321 to 1203 BCE, across both.

events.description: Hittite king Mursili II binds neighbouring rulers, such as Duppi-Teššup of Amurru, by written treaties.
events.significance: Treaties of this kind open by naming the great king and what he had done. Some scholars compare the Ten Commandments, which open “who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (king c. 1321–1295 BC, short chronology; "Treaty of Muršili II with Duppi-Teššup of Amurru")
Wikipedia, "Covenant (biblical)" (the Decalogue "begins with Yahweh's identification and what he had done for Israel", like a suzerainty treaty; Weinfeld sees the Mosaic covenant as one)
Exodus 20:2

events.description: Pharaoh Horemheb's Great Edict names two judges, for the south and the north of Egypt, and orders them not to take bribes.
events.significance: In Yitro, Jethro advises Moses to appoint judges who are trustworthy and “hate unjust gain” (Exodus 18:21).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Great Edict of Horemheb" (penalties for officials who seize a poor man's goods; judges appointed and told not to take bribes; a judge who "commits a crime against justice" commits "a capital crime")
Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled "between 1319 BC and 1292 BC"; authored the Edict of Horemheb)
Exodus 18:21

events.description: At Deir el-Medina, the village of Egypt's royal tomb-builders, the working week is eight days followed by two days off. Under Merneptah, with festivals, over a third of the year is time off.
events.significance: The fourth commandment sets every seventh day as a day of rest, for servants and animals too (Exodus 20:8–10).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Deir el-Medina" ("The working week was eight days followed by two days holiday"; over a third of the year off "during the reign of Merneptah (c. 1213–1203 BC)")
Exodus 20:8-10

mishpatim.note: Tradition dates these laws to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1319 to 1187 BCE, across both.

events.description: Horemheb's Great Edict punishes officials who seize a poor man's goods, and makes it a capital crime for a judge to pervert justice.
events.significance: Mishpatim also commands: do not twist the judgment of the poor, and take no bribe, “for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted” (Exodus 23:6–8).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Great Edict of Horemheb" (penalties for officials who seize a poor man's goods; judges appointed and told not to take bribes; a judge who "commits a crime against justice" commits "a capital crime")
Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled "between 1319 BC and 1292 BC"; authored the Edict of Horemheb)
Exodus 23:6-8

events.description: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III swear a treaty before “a thousand gods”, with curses for whoever breaks it and blessings for whoever keeps it.
events.significance: In Mishpatim, Moses writes down the laws, reads “the book of the covenant” to the people, and they swear to keep it (Exodus 24:4–8).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty" (around 1259 BC; oath before "a thousand gods, male gods and female gods"; curses and blessings)
Exodus 24:4-8

events.description: An Egyptian frontier official reports letting Shasu tribes of Edom pass a fort in Tjeku to the lakes of Pithom, “to keep them alive and to keep their flocks alive”.
events.significance: Mishpatim twice forbids oppressing the stranger, “for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:20; 23:9).

sources.title: Manfred Bietak and Gary A. Rendsburg, "Egypt and the Exodus," in Ancient Israel, ed. H. Shanks (Biblical Archaeology Society): P. Anastasi VI, report of a frontier official, "year 8" (they date the papyrus to Seti II's reign; others to year 8 of Merneptah)
Exodus 23:9

events.description: Emar, a trading city on the Euphrates in Syria, is destroyed. Its tablets, mostly from the 13th century, are private and legal records: sales, court cases, wills, adoptions.
events.significance: They show everyday law at work: property, family and disputes, the same ground many of Mishpatim's rules cover.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Emar" (texts from the 14th century BC "to the fall of Emar in 1187 BC"; tablets record "private transactions, judicial records, dealings in real estate, marriages, last wills, formal adoptions")

terumah.note: Tradition dates the command to build the Tabernacle to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1329 to 1290 BCE, across both.

events.description: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela orders new statues of the gods in fine electrum, and new processional boats of Lebanese cedar decorated with gold and silver.
events.significance: It raises the number of carrying poles for Amun's image from 7 to 13. The ark in Terumah is also carried on poles (Exodus 25:13–15).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Restoration Stela" (Amun made "13 poles long ... although ... only 7 poles long before"; Aidan Dodson dates it to "Year 4")
Colleen Darnell, "A Highlight of the GEM: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela" (statues "of the finest electrum"; barks "of the best cedar from Lebanon and decorated with gold and silver")
Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (ruled c. 1332–1323 BC)
Exodus 25:13-15

events.description: Tutankhamun is buried with a gilded wooden shrine topped by a jackal of the god Anubis, mounted on a base with two carrying poles.
events.significance: The ark was a gold-covered wooden chest carried on poles. Scott Noegel argues that Egyptian sacred barques, carried on poles, are a more plausible model for it than Bedouin sacred chests.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Anubis Shrine" (wood covered with gold leaf; "two carrying poles")
Wikipedia, "Ark of the Covenant" (Noegel: the Egyptian solar barque "a more plausible model")
Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (ruled c. 1332–1323 BC)
Exodus 25:10-14

events.description: At Timna, a copper-mining valley in the Arabah north of the Gulf of Aqaba, a small temple to Hathor is built for Egyptian miners. Its excavator dates it to Seti I; Ramesses II rebuilt it.
events.significance: Scholars such as Mark S. Smith and William Dever think the Tabernacle was based on portable tent shrines known across the region. A Midianite tent shrine of Hathor at Timna is one example.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Timna Valley" ("approximately 30 kilometres ... north of the Gulf of Aqaba"; Rothenberg: temple for "the Egyptian miners", built "during the reign of Pharaoh Seti I"; rebuilt under Ramses II)
Wikipedia, "Tabernacle" (Smith, Dever: based on tent shrines; "The Midianite tent shrine of Hathor at Timna")

tetzaveh.note: Tradition dates the command for the priests' garments to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1320 to 1213 BCE, across both.

events.description: A merchant ship sinks off southern Turkey. Its cargo includes cylinder seals carved from rock crystal and hematite, and cobalt-blue glass ingots.
events.significance: The high priest's shoulder stones are engraved with the tribes' names “like the engravings of a signet” (Exodus 28:11).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Uluburun shipwreck" (late 14th century BC; sinking dated "1320±15"; "Nine ancient Near Eastern cylinder seals" of rock crystal, faience, hematite; 175 glass ingots of cobalt blue, turquoise, lavender)
Exodus 28:11

events.description: In his first year, Ramesses II names Nebwenenef High Priest of Amun and gives him two gold signet rings and a staff of office. His son later succeeds him as High Priest of Hathor.
events.significance: In Tetzaveh, Aaron and his sons are made priests, and the priesthood passes to Aaron's sons “for all time” (Exodus 29:9).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Nebwenenef" (appointed "in Year 1, III Akhet of Ramesses II"; "two gold signet rings and an electrum staff of office"; son Sematawy II became High Priest of Hathor)
Exodus 29:9

events.description: Bakenkhonsu, High Priest of Amun, dies at about 90. His statue lists his rise through the priestly ranks, from ordinary priest to high priest for 27 years.
events.significance: Egypt's priests held ranks, from the ordinary wab-priest up. Tetzaveh also sets the high priest apart from the other priests by his garments (Exodus 28).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Bakenkhonsu" ("died in the last regnal year of Ramesses II, at the age of ninety"; wab priest, prophets, High Priest "for 27 years")
Exodus 28:1-4

ki-tisa.note: Tradition dates the golden calf to c. 1313 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1321 to 1250 BCE, across both.

events.description: Hittite king Mursili II makes written treaties with neighbouring rulers, among them Duppi-Teššup of Amurru and Niqmepa of Ugarit.
events.significance: Some scholars compare the Sinai covenant to such treaties. In Ki Tisa, after the calf, God renews the covenant and Moses writes its words again (Exodus 34:10, 27–28).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (king c. 1321–1295 BC, short chronology; treaties with Duppi-Teššup of Amurru and Niqmepa of Ugarit)
Wikipedia, "Covenant (biblical)" (the Decalogue "begins with Yahweh's identification and what he had done for Israel", like a suzerainty treaty; Weinfeld sees the Mosaic covenant as one)
Exodus 34:27-28

events.description: The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty is first written on silver tablets, one given to each side. Copies survive on Egyptian temple walls and Hittite clay tablets.
events.significance: The covenant in Ki Tisa is also written on tablets, “the two tablets of the testimony” (Exodus 31:18).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty" (around 1259 BC; "now-lost silver tablets, which were given to each side")
Exodus 31:18

events.description: At Saqqara, Ramesses II's son Khaemweset oversees the burials of sacred Apis bulls, in years 16 and 30 of his father's reign, with gilded coffins and gold foil.
events.significance: Egyptians honoured the Apis bull with rich burials. In Ki Tisa, Israel makes a golden calf (Exodus 32:4); the Torah does not say it copied any Egyptian cult.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Serapeum of Saqqara" ("Isolated Tomb G/H – Ramesses II, years 16 & 30"; overseen by Khaemweset; coffins with lower halves gilt, "gold foil")
Exodus 32:4

vayakhel.note: Tradition dates the building of the Tabernacle to c. 1313–1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1320 to 1244 BCE, across both.

events.description: The Uluburun ship sinks with ten tons of copper and a ton of tin, enough for about eleven tons of bronze, plus ebony, ivory and glass.
events.significance: In Vayakhel, the people bring gold, silver and copper, and more than enough is given (Exodus 35:5; 36:5–7).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Uluburun shipwreck" (late 14th century BC; sinking dated "1320±15"; "Raw copper cargo totaling ten tons"; "Approximately one ton of tin" making "about 11 tons of bronze"; blackwood (ebony), ivory)
Exodus 35:5

events.description: Seti I begins a temple of white limestone at Abydos, known for its fine carved reliefs. His son Ramesses II completes it.
events.significance: Vayakhel names Bezalel and Oholiab as master craftsmen, skilled in carving, weaving and metalwork (Exodus 35:30–35).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruled 1290–1279 BC; "a magnificent temple made of white limestone at Abydos featuring exquisite relief scenes was started by Seti, and later completed by his son")
Exodus 35:30-35

events.description: Work begins on the great rock-cut temple at Abu Simbel. It takes about twenty years, and is aligned so the sun lights the sanctuary statues on two days a year.
events.significance: The Tabernacle, by contrast, is a tent built to be taken down and carried. Vayakhel records its making piece by piece (Exodus 36–38).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Abu Simbel" (construction "started in c. 1264 BC" and lasted "until 1244 BC"; sun penetrates the sanctuary "on October 22 and February 22")
Exodus 36:8

pekudei.note: Tradition dates the setting up of the Tabernacle to c. 1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1332 to 1187 BCE, across both.

events.description: Kurigalzu II rules Babylon for about 25 years. 167 business records, mostly from Nippur, are dated to his reign; an accountant in his service owns a cylinder seal.
events.significance: Pekudei opens with an audit: “These are the accounts of the Tabernacle”, listing the gold, silver and copper used (Exodus 38:21–31).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Kurigalzu II" (c. 1332–1308 BC; "167 economic texts, mostly from Nippur"; cylinder seals of servants "such as the accountant, Uballissu-Marduk")
Exodus 38:21

events.description: Under Pharaoh Merneptah, an Egyptian papyrus keeps a ledger of building works, including brickmaking.
events.significance: Pekudei's accounts also track materials for a building project, down to the silver for its sockets and hooks (Exodus 38:27–28).

sources.title: Manfred Bietak and Gary A. Rendsburg, "Egypt and the Exodus," in Ancient Israel, ed. H. Shanks (Biblical Archaeology Society): "P. Anastasi III (verso) 1.2–3.3, dated to the reign of Merneptah ... includes a ledger of sorts recording various building works, including the making of bricks"
Wikipedia, "Merneptah" (reigned 1213–1203 BCE)
Exodus 38:27-28

events.description: Emar in Syria falls. A priest's library there held ritual texts for the local cults, among them a rite for installing the high priestess of the storm god Baal.
events.significance: Pekudei ends with the priests' garments made and the Tabernacle set up and anointed (Exodus 39–40), rites that Leviticus then carries out.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Emar" (texts from the 14th century BC "to the fall of Emar in 1187 BC"; "In the house of a priest, a library contained ... ritual texts for local cults"; Daniel E. Fleming, The Installation of Baal's High Priestess at Emar (1992))
Exodus 40:9
Daniel E. Fleming, The Installation of Baal's High Priestess at Emar (Harvard Semitic Studies 42, 1992)

tzav.note: Tradition dates the seven days of the priests' ordination to c. 1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1319 to 1272 BCE, across both.

events.description: Pharaoh Horemheb's coronation inscription says he rebuilt ruined temples, remade the damaged statues of the gods, and staffed Amun's temples with priests chosen from the army.
events.significance: In Tzav, Moses installs Aaron and his sons as priests in a ceremony lasting seven days (Leviticus 8:2, 8:33).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled "between 1319 BC and 1292 BC"; coronation inscription: statues of the old gods remade, temples rebuilt, "servants to the god and lector priests from the military elite")
Leviticus 8:33

events.description: Seti I builds the Great Hypostyle Hall in the temple of Amun at Karnak. Its roof rested on 134 columns; his son Ramesses II finished carving its southern half.
events.significance: Tzav sets out the priests' daily duties at the altar, such as keeping its fire burning, and their share of the offerings (Leviticus 6–7).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Great Hypostyle Hall" ("134 columns"; "built entirely by Seti I"; southern wing's decoration "completed by his son and successor ... Ramesses II")
Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruling "1290 BC to 1279 BC")

events.description: Hittite king Muwatalli II's model prayer sets out, on a roof, “35 thick breads” of moist flour and “a thin bowl of honey mixed with fine oil”. The offerings are then burnt.
events.significance: Tzav's grain offering is choice flour and oil, burnt on the altar (Leviticus 6:7–8). Leviticus bars honey from any offering burnt to God (2:11).

sources.title: Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (Society of Biblical Literature, 2002), no. 20: Muwatalli II "(c. 1295–1272)"; §1 breads and "honey mixed with fine oil"; offerings "burnt on the roof (§93)"
Leviticus 6:7–8
Leviticus 2:11

shemini.note: Tradition dates the eighth day, when the priests began their service, to c. 1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1321 to 1237 BCE, across both.

events.description: Hittite king Mursili II complains that scribes and temple staff kept changing the rites set for the Goddess of the Night at Samuha. He restores them from the tablets.
events.significance: Shemini tells of Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu, who offered “alien fire—which had not been enjoined upon them” (Leviticus 10:1).

sources.title: Jared L. Miller, "Setting Up the Goddess of the Night Separately" (2008): Mursili II "(last third of the fourteenth century)"; "the wooden tablet scribes and the temple personnel began incessantly to alter them ... I, Mursili, Great King, have re-edited them from the tablets"
Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (king "1321–1295 BC (short chronology)")
Leviticus 10:1

events.description: Hittite king Hattusili III founds a second cult for his patron goddess, Ishtar of Samuha, in the town of Urikina.
events.significance: Shemini describes the first day of worship at the newly set-up Tabernacle, on “the eighth day” (Leviticus 9:1).

sources.title: Jared L. Miller, "Setting Up the Goddess of the Night Separately" (2008): "Hattusili III even further “split” Ishtar of Samuha in order to found an additional cult for her in the town of Urikina"
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002): Hattusili III "(c. 1267–1237)"
Leviticus 9:1

events.description: At Mycenae in Greece, a gate topped by two carved lions is built as the main entrance to the citadel.
events.significance: The Lion Gate is the largest surviving sculpture of the Bronze Age Aegean. It shows the wider world of the time; the Torah does not mention it.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Lion Gate" ("erected during the thirteenth century BC, around 1250 BC"; "the largest surviving sculpture in the Bronze Age Aegean")

tazria.note: The Torah gives no date for these laws, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1267 to 1237 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: Hattusili III, the Hittite king, asks Ramesses II for medicine so his sister, aged 50 or 60, can bear children. Ramesses doubts it can work, but sends a physician and an exorcist.
events.significance: Tazria opens with the laws for a woman who has given birth (Leviticus 12:2).

sources.title: Diacrítica 37:2 (2023), "Beyond Amarna: Exorcists without Borders in the Levant": Hattusili asks for "a man to prepare a medicine so that she may bear children!"; "One can't produce medicine to enable her to bear children!"; he sends "a competent āšipu and a competent a[sû]"
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002): Hattusili III "(c. 1267–1237)"
Leviticus 12:2

events.description: In China, Shang kings ask their ancestors questions by cracking ox bones and turtle shells, then carve them: the earliest large body of Chinese writing. Some ask about Queen Fu Hao's childbirth.
events.significance: The start date is debated; bones from King Wu Ding's reign are radiocarbon-dated to 1254–1197 BCE. Their topics include illness and birth, the subjects of Tazria.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Oracle bone" ("Late Shang period (c. 1250 – c. 1050 BCE)"; "the earliest known significant corpus of ancient Chinese writing"; topics "from illness, birth and death"; 26 bones "radiocarbon dated to 1254–1197 BCE (±10 years)")
Wikipedia, "Fu Hao" ("Oracle bone divinations by Nan show concern for her well-being at the time of the birth")

events.description: In his 34th year, Ramesses II marries a daughter of Hattusili III and Queen Puduhepa, who becomes his chief queen.
events.significance: The marriage concluded the peace begun with the treaty of 1259 BCE. Letters between the two courts also dealt with doctors and childbirth, as with Hattusili's sister.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Maathorneferure" (daughter of Hattusili III and Puduhepa; "married to the Egyptian Pharaoh Ramesses II in his Year 34, becoming a senior queen, the King's Great Wife")
Wikipedia, "Ramesses II" (reign 1279–1213 BCE; year 34 ≈ 1246)

metzora.note: The Torah gives no date for these laws, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1267 to 1213 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: Hittite king Hattusili III writes that he was a sickly child, not expected to live, and credits the goddess Ishtar with saving his life.
events.significance: Metzora gives the rites for someone healed of skin disease: washing, shaving and bathing, then offerings on the eighth day (Leviticus 14:8–10).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Ḫattušili III" (king "1267–1237 BC (short chronology)"; the Apology, written "during his reign"; "an ill and sickly child who was initially expected not to survive"; "credited the goddess Ishtar with saving his life")
Leviticus 14:8–10

events.description: A register of absences at Deir el-Medina, Egypt's tomb-builders' village, gives reasons: illness, eye disease, a scorpion sting, and a wife's or daughter's menstruation, literally “purification”.
events.significance: Leviticus 15 sets rules for bodily discharges, including seven days of “menstrual separation” (15:19).

sources.title: University of Hamburg, CSMC, Manuscript of the Month 54, "Stung by a scorpion" (BM EA 5634, year 40 of Ramesses II, "c. 1250 BCE"; "His daughter was in menstruation (literally, in purification)"; "ill"; eye disease; scorpion)
Leviticus 15:19

events.description: Ramesses II writes to the Hittite court, apparently to Tudhaliya IV and his mother Puduhepa, that he is sending an Egyptian physician, Pariamahu, to cure Kurunta of an illness.
events.significance: In Metzora the priest does not treat the disease. He goes “outside the camp” to see whether it has healed (Leviticus 14:3).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Kurunta (king)" (an "Insibia letter" from Ramesses II to "(apparently) Tudḫaliya IV and his mother Puduḫepa records the special dispatch of an Egyptian physician, Pariamaḫu, to cure Kurunta")
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002): Tudhaliya IV "(c. 1237–1209)"
Leviticus 14:3

acharei-mot.note: Tradition dates these laws, given after the death of Aaron's sons, to c. 1312 BCE. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1312 to 1185 BCE, across both.

events.description: A Hittite ritual for Mursili II's ailing queen sends the god Lelwani a fattened cow and ewe as her “substitutes”, inviting the god to eat their fat and drink their blood.
events.significance: Acharei Mot forbids eating blood: “the life of the flesh is in the blood”, which God assigns to the altar for expiation (Leviticus 17:11–12).

sources.title: Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002), no. 15, Mursili's Prayer to Lelwani (CTH 380): the queen died "probably in his ninth year of rule"; "her substitutes: [one fattened cow,] and one fattened ewe"; "eat the fat"
Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (king "1321–1295 BC (short chronology)")
Leviticus 17:10–12

events.description: Hittite king Muwatalli II prays to the Storm-god over the decline of Kummanni, confessing wrongs and asking him to hear “how I dispel the sins of the lands”.
events.significance: On the Day of Atonement Aaron confesses over the live goat “all the iniquities and transgressions of the Israelites” (Leviticus 16:21).

sources.title: Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002), no. 19, Muwatalli's Prayer Concerning the Cult of Kummanni (CTH 382): "a typical plea of confession and penitence"; §1; Muwatalli II "(c. 1295–1272)"
Leviticus 16:21

events.description: At Ugarit in Syria, a rite copied several times offers sacrifices on behalf of the kingdom's men and women for sins committed “in your anger”, in impatience or in sacrifices.
events.significance: Some compare it with the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:30). Its editor, Dennis Pardee, cautions that the differences are important and allow only general comparison.

sources.title: Dennis Pardee, Ritual and Cult at Ugarit (SBL, 2002), text 22 (RS 1.002): male and female inhabitants; "whether you sin: be it in your anger"; "Comparisons with the biblical Day of Atonement are tempting, but the important differences..."; most sacrificial texts date "to the years 1200–1185 in round figures"
Leviticus 16:30

kedoshim.note: The Torah gives no date for these laws, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1300 to 1200 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: At Deir el-Medina, the workman Neferabu dedicates a stela to Ptah: “I am a man who swore falsely by Ptah, Lord of Maat, and he made me see darkness by day.”
events.significance: Kedoshim commands: “You shall not swear falsely by My name” (Leviticus 19:12).

sources.title: British Museum Images, "Stela, 19th Dynasty, Deir el-Medina" (BM EA 589, stela of Neferabu to Ptah; "13th century bc")
Miriam Lichtheim, Ancient Egyptian Literature II (1976), "Votive Stela of Neferabu with Hymn to Ptah" ("I am a man who swore falsely by Ptah, Lord of Maat, And he made me see darkness by day")
Leviticus 19:12

events.description: The Book of the Dead made for the Theban scribe Ani lists wrongs he denies before the gods' judges, including “I have not stolen” and “I have not uttered lies”.
events.significance: Kedoshim's commands include “You shall not steal; you shall not deal deceitfully or falsely with one another” (Leviticus 19:11).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Papyrus of Ani" ("created c. 1250 BCE"; made "for the Theban scribe Ani")
Joshua J. Mark, "The Negative Confession", World History Encyclopedia (Budge's translation from the Papyrus of Ani: "I have not stolen", "I have not uttered lies")
Leviticus 19:11

events.description: A merchant ship sinks off Cape Gelidonya in southern Turkey. Its cargo includes copper and tin ingots and pan-balance weights that follow Near Eastern standards.
events.significance: Kedoshim requires “an honest balance, honest weights” (Leviticus 19:36).

sources.title: American Journal of Archaeology 125.3 (2021), necrology of George F. Bass ("pan-balance weights found in the wreck adhered to Near Eastern standards"; sank "around 1200 BCE")
Institute of Nautical Archaeology, "Cape Gelidonya Late Bronze Age Shipwreck Excavation" ("In about 1200 B.C."; stone weights)
Wikipedia, "Cape Gelidonya" (copper and tin ingots, "merchant weights")
Leviticus 19:35–36

emor.note: The Torah gives no date for these laws, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1279 to 1209 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: Ramesses II builds his memorial temple at Thebes, the Ramesseum, over about 20 years. Its reliefs show the festival of Min, held at the start of the harvest.
events.significance: Emor's calendar marks the harvest's start: “you shall bring the first sheaf of your harvest to the priest” (Leviticus 23:10).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Ramesseum" (work "began shortly after the start of his reign and continued for 20 years"; reliefs of "a feast in honour of" Min and "ceremonies of the festival of Min")
Wikipedia, "Min (god)" ("At the beginning of the harvest season ... the Min Festival, when they blessed the harvest")
Leviticus 23:10

events.description: Ramesses II holds his first Sed festival, a royal feast of renewal held after 30 years on the throne. He will hold more than a dozen.
events.significance: Emor's festivals are set by the calendar, “each at its appointed time” (Leviticus 23:4), not by the years of a king.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Sed festival" (celebrated "after a ruler had held the throne for thirty years"; Ramesses II "had his first of over a dozen in approximately 1249 BCE")
Leviticus 23:4

events.description: Tablets of instructions are prepared for Hittite queen Puduhepa for the hišuwa, a nine-day festival from Kizzuwatna in southern Anatolia, her homeland.
events.significance: Emor's Feast of Booths lasts seven days, with a sacred occasion on the eighth (Leviticus 23:34–36).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Manuzi" ("nine day hišuwa festival, known from a set of tablets with instructions pertaining to it prepared for queen Puduḫepa")
Wikipedia, "Puduḫepa" (born "in the city of Lawazantiya in Kizzuwatna (i.e. Cilicia...)"; queen of Hattusili III, still prominent under Tudhaliya IV)
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002): Hattusili III "(c. 1267–1237)", Tudhaliya IV "(c. 1237–1209)"
Leviticus 23:34–36

behar.note: The Torah says these laws were given “on Mount Sinai” (25:1) but gives no date, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1262 to 1209 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: An Egyptian family's court fight over land granted by King Ahmose I centuries before goes on. In year 18 of Ramesses II a widow loses; her son Mose sues to win it back.
events.significance: Behar treats family land as a lasting inheritance: in the jubilee year “each of you shall return to your holding” (Leviticus 25:10).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mose (scribe)" (land granted under Ahmose I to Neshi; widow Nubnofret "lost at the court against Khay. This happened in year 18 under Ramesses II"; Mose "tried to claim the land back")
Wikipedia, "Ramesses II" (reign 1279–1213 BCE; year 18 ≈ 1262)
Leviticus 25:10

events.description: After a drought, Hittite king Tudhaliya IV has dams built across his empire, a cuneiform text records. A dam near Alaca Höyük, dedicated to the goddess Hepat, is probably one.
events.significance: Behar asks, “What are we to eat in the seventh year?” and promises a sixth-year crop “sufficient for three years” (Leviticus 25:20–21).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Gölpınar Dam" ("Tudhaliya IV ... had ten dams built in the Hittite empire around 1240 BC after a period of drought"; inscription dedicating it to Ḫepat)
Leviticus 25:20–22
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (Society of Biblical Literature, 2002): Tudhaliya IV "(c. 1237–1209)"

events.description: Hittite king Tudhaliya IV confirms Kurunta as king of Tarhuntassa in a treaty on a bronze tablet, fixing his borders and granting more land. It was found at Hattusa in 1986.
events.significance: Behar limits the sale of land, “for the land is Mine; you are but strangers resident with Me” (Leviticus 25:23).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Kurunta (king)" (Tudhaliya's treaty "inscribed on a bronze tablet, discovered at Ḫattuša in 1986"; frontiers "in greater detail", "award or return of additional territories")
Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002): Tudhaliya IV "(c. 1237–1209)"
Leviticus 25:23

bechukotai.note: The Torah gives no date for these blessings, warnings and laws, and scholars place them differently; many date the writing of Leviticus much later. These events run from c. 1267 to 1203 BCE, inside the 13th century BCE, where scholars who date the Exodus usually place it. They show that world; the Torah names none of them.

events.description: Hittite queen Puduhepa prays for her sick husband, Hattusili III, vowing the goddess Lelwani a silver statue of him “as big as Hattusili himself”, with head, hands and feet of gold.
events.significance: Leviticus 27 sets silver values for vowing a person: fifty shekels for a man aged twenty to sixty (27:2–3).

sources.title: Itamar Singer, Hittite Prayers (2002), no. 22: Puduhepa "prays for the recuperation of her ailing husband"; §9″ "a silver statue of Hattusili, as big as Hattusili himself, with its head, its hands and its feet of gold"; Hattusili III "(c. 1267–1237)"
Leviticus 27:2–4

events.description: Assyrian king Tukulti-Ninurta I captures Babylon, takes its king Kashtiliashu IV to Assyria in chains, and carries off the statue of the god Marduk from its temple.
events.significance: Leviticus 26 warns of cities in ruin, sanctuaries made desolate and a people scattered “among the nations” (26:31–33).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Kaštiliašu IV" (king "c. 1232–1225 BC", "ruled for eight years"; captured and "deported him ignominiously in chains to Assyria"; "made off with the statue of Marduk")
Wikipedia, "Tukulti-Ninurta I" ("reigned c. 1243–1207 BC")
Leviticus 26:31–33

events.description: Pharaoh Merneptah boasts, in a long inscription at Karnak, that he has “caused grain to be sent in ships” to keep the famine-struck Hittite land alive.
events.significance: Leviticus 26 threatens famine, when “they shall dole out your bread by weight” (26:26).

sources.title: Colleen Manassa, The Great Karnak Inscription of Merneptah (2003), line 24: "It is in order to vivify this Hittite land that I have caused grain to be sent in ships"
Israel Knohl, "Joseph and the Famine", TheTorah.com (Merneptah, 1213–1203 B.C.E.: "he caused grain to be taken in ships, to keep alive this land of Hatti")
Leviticus 26:26

bamidbar.note: Tradition dates the census to c. 1312 BCE, in the second year after the Exodus. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1321 to 1279 BCE, across both.

events.description: Mursili II becomes king of the Hittites. His annals record his enemies' taunt: “your infantry and chariotry are few. Against your infantry, I have many infantry.”
events.significance: Kings measured their strength in soldiers. Bamidbar opens by counting Israel's men “from the age of twenty years up… who are able to bear arms” (1:3).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Mursili II" ("In 1321 BC Mursili II assumed the Hittite throne"; the taunt quoted from his Annals)
Numbers 1:3

events.description: In Seti I's first year, towns near Beth-Shean in Canaan rebel. His stela there says he sent three divisions of his army, named for the gods Amun, Re and Seth.
events.significance: Bamidbar also arranges Israel in divisions: the tribes camp “each under its standard” around the Tent of Meeting (1:52; 2:2).

sources.title: Israel Museum, Pharaoh in Canaan catalogue, "Stela ('First Stela') of Seti I" ("Year 1"; "the king dispatched three divisions of his army to put down the revolt – the division of Amun… the division of Re… and the division of Sutekh (Seth)")
Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruling 1290 BC to 1279 BC; "A stele in Beth-Shan testifies to that reconquest")
Numbers 1:52
Numbers 2:2

events.description: Seti I's decree at Nauri, in Nubia, protects the workers of his temple at Abydos: they may not be conscripted for other labor, and their animals may not be taken.
events.significance: Bamidbar also sets sanctuary workers apart: the Levites are not counted with the fighting men (1:49) but put in charge of the Tabernacle (1:50).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Temple of Seti I (Abydos)" (the Nauri decree: "the workers were unable to be conscripted for labor or have their animals taken")
Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruling 1290 BC to 1279 BC)
Numbers 1:49-50

nasso.note: Tradition dates the chieftains' gifts to c. 1312 BCE, when the Tabernacle was set up. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1313 to 1279 BCE, across both.

events.description: In his seventh year, Pharaoh Horemheb reorganizes the workforce of Deir el-Medina, the village of the craftsmen who cut and decorate the royal tombs.
events.significance: Nasso finishes counting the Levite clans and gives each man “his service and porterage” in carrying the Tabernacle (4:49).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled "between 1319 BC and 1292 BC"; "reorganized the Deir el-Medina workforce in his 7th year")
Wikipedia, "Deir el-Medina" (workers "involved in the administration and decoration of the royal tombs")
Numbers 4:49

events.description: About ten years into his reign, Hittite king Mursili II demotes and banishes his stepmother, a Babylonian princess, after an oracle finds her guilty of causing his wife's death.
events.significance: Nasso's sotah law also leaves a hidden wrong, where “there is no witness” (5:13), to a divine test. The charge differs: a wife suspected of adultery.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Šuppiluliuma I" (the Babylonian Tawananna "would survive a decade into the reign" of Muršili II, "who would demote and banish her after an oracle confirmed that she was guilty of causing the death of the king's wife")
Wikipedia, "Mursili II" (throne in 1321 BC)
Numbers 5:13

events.description: Seti I dies and is buried in the Valley of the Kings. The wine jars in his tomb are labeled by year of his reign, none later than year 8.
events.significance: Wine went with a king to his grave. In Nasso, a Nazirite vows to “abstain from wine” and to eat no grapes, “fresh or dried” (6:3).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Seti I" (ruling 1290 BC to 1279 BC; "no wine labels higher than Seti I's 8th regnal year were found in his KV17 tomb")
Numbers 6:3

behaalotecha.note: Tradition dates the departure from Sinai to c. 1312 BCE, in the second year. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1332 to 1292 BCE, across both.

events.description: Huy serves as Tutankhamun's viceroy of Kush. His tomb at Thebes shows envoys and chiefs of Kush bringing animal skins, giraffe tails and captives.
events.significance: Behaalotecha tells of Moses' “Cushite” wife (12:1). In the Bible, Cush is usually the land south of Egypt, Nubia; who she was is debated.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Amenhotep called Huy" ("Viceroy of Kush under 18th Dynasty King Tutankhamen"; "chieftains from Wawat and Kush presenting offerings to Huy, including animal skins, giraffes' tails, and captives")
Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (ruled c. 1332 – 1323 BC)
Wikipedia, "Cush (Bible)" (Cush "generally understood in biblical geography to lie south of Egypt, corresponding to Nubia"; the woman's identity "has been widely debated")
Numbers 12:1

events.description: Tutankhamun is buried with a pair of trumpets, one silver and one bronze or copper, the oldest working trumpets known. They were likely used for military signals.
events.significance: Behaalotecha orders “two silver trumpets” to summon the community and “set the divisions in motion” (10:2).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun's trumpets" ("a pair of trumpets", "one of sterling silver and one of bronze or copper", "the oldest operational trumpets in the world"; "likely played on a single note for military signalling")
Wikipedia, "Tutankhamun" (c. 1342 BC – c. 1323 BC)
Numbers 10:2

events.description: Pharaoh Horemheb restores the priesthood of Amun, but appoints priests who mostly come from the army, men whose loyalty he can rely on.
events.significance: Behaalotecha sets the Levites apart to serve at the Tabernacle, taken by God “in place of” Israel's firstborn (8:16).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Horemheb" (ruled between 1319 BC and 1292 BC; "reappointing priests who mostly came from the Egyptian army since he could rely on their personal loyalty")
Numbers 8:16

shelach.note: Tradition dates the spies' mission to c. 1312 BCE, in the second year. Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1332 to 1213 BCE, across both.

events.description: In the tomb of Huy, Tutankhamun's viceroy, chiefs of Retjenu, Egypt's name for Canaan and Syria, bring horses, lapis, gold, silver and copper, which Huy delivers to the king.
events.significance: Canaan was then under Egyptian rule. In Shelach the spies bring back the land's own produce: grapes, pomegranates and figs (13:23).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Amenhotep called Huy" ("Retenu chiefs present horses, lapis, gold, silver, and copper which Huy is later depicted delivering to King Tutankhamun")
Wikipedia, "Retjenu" ("the Ancient Egyptian name for the wider Syrian region, where the Semitic-speaking Canaanites lived")
Wikipedia, "Beit She'an" ("When Canaan came under Imperial Egyptian rule in the Late Bronze Age")
Numbers 13:23

events.description: Ramesses II besieges Dapur in Syria. Reliefs in his temple at Thebes show a hilltop town with inner and outer walls, and Egyptian soldiers climbing scaling ladders.
events.significance: The spies report that “the cities are fortified and very large” (13:28).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Dapur" (siege "in 1269 BC"; "a heavily fortified settlement with both inner and outer walls and situated on a rocky hill"; "soldiers climbing scale ladders")
Wikipedia, "Ramesses II" (sieges of Dapur in his eighth and tenth years)
Numbers 13:28

events.description: An Egyptian scribe's satirical letter, composed under Ramesses II, warns a colleague of a narrow pass hiding Shasu nomads “of four cubits or of five cubits,” “fierce of face.”
events.significance: The spies say they saw giants, “and we looked like grasshoppers to ourselves” (13:33). The letter is satire; its editor, Alan Gardiner, allowed for “Egyptian exaggeration.”

sources.title: Alan H. Gardiner, Egyptian Hieratic Texts I: Literary Texts of the New Kingdom (1911), Papyrus Anastasi I ("written certainly not earlier, but probably also not later, than the reign of Rameses II"; Shosu "of four cubits or of five cubits… fierce of face"; "with due allowance for Egyptian exaggeration")
Wikipedia, "Papyrus Anastasi I" (satirical letter of the scribe Hori to Amenemope)
Numbers 13:33

korach.note: The Torah does not date Korach's rebellion, and tradition gives it no year (Seder Olam places it after the spies). Scholars who date the Exodus usually place it in the 13th century BCE, and many doubt it can be dated. These events run from c. 1279 to 1200 BCE, inside that range.

events.description: Ramesses II names Nebwenenef High Priest of Amun. The king says he read out names of courtiers and priests before the god, who accepted none until he named Nebwenenef.
events.significance: In Korach, the choice of priest is also left to God: “The staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout” (17:20; 17:5 in many English Bibles).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Nebwenenef" (appointed "in Year 1, III Akhet of Ramesses II"; "he was not satisfied with any of them, until I mentioned your name to him")
Wikipedia, "Ramesses II" (accession "31 May 1279 BC")
Numbers 17:20

events.description: Hattusili rebels against his nephew, Hittite king Urhi-Teshub, and takes the throne. He says he wrote to him: “Istar of Samuha and the Storm God of Nerik shall decide the case for us!”
events.significance: Moses also leaves the decision to God: “Come morning, GOD will make known who is to serve” (16:5).

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Hattusili III" (king c. 1267–1237 BC (short chronology); "He served his brother Muwatalli II and his nephew Mursili III before rebelling and taking the throne")
Wikipedia, "Mursili III" (Urhi-Teshub; the Apology: "Since I wrote to Urhi-Tesub in this manner"; "Istar of Samuha and the Storm God of Nerik shall decide the case for us!")
Numbers 16:5

events.description: Amenmesse seizes power in southern Egypt, probably as a rival to Pharaoh Seti II. After Seti II wins back Thebes, his agents erase Amenmesse's name from his tomb.
events.significance: Korach and his allies also challenge those in power: “Why then do you raise yourselves above GOD's congregation?” (16:3).

events.description: At Emar, on the Euphrates in Syria, most tablets from this century are private records, including wills. There a daughter could be treated like a son and inherit from her father.

events.description: Babylon's king Kadashman-Enlil II tells the Hittite king Hattusili III why his envoys stopped coming: “Since the Ahlamu are hostile I have stopped sending my messengers.”
events.significance: The Ahlamu were semi-nomads of the Syrian steppe; later texts call such groups Arameans. The first-fruits declaration begins: “My father was a fugitive Aramean” (26:5).

events.description: Assyria's Tukulti-Ninurta I defeats Babylon's king Kashtiliash IV, carries off the statue of the god Marduk, and sends the captive king into exile.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 28:36 warns that God “will drive you, and the king you have set over you, to a nation unknown to you or your ancestors.”

events.description: Assyrian king Shalmaneser I absorbs what is left of the kingdom of Mitanni. He is one of the first Assyrian kings known to deport defeated enemies to other lands.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 29:27 pictures a people uprooted “from their soil” and cast “into another land” for abandoning the covenant.

events.description: Early in his reign, Hittite king Hattusili III makes his nephew Kurunta king of Tarhuntassa. The treaty promises that Kurunta's son and grandson will keep the throne if loyal.
events.significance: The treaty calls on divine and human witnesses. Moses says: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day” (30:19).

events.description: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III make a peace treaty that binds not only themselves but their children and grandchildren.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 29:13–14 makes the covenant “not with you alone” but also “with those who are not with us here this day.”

events.description: Hittite king Muwatalli II makes a treaty with Alaksandu, king of Wilusa in western Anatolia. It says the tablet “shall be read out before you three times yearly.”
events.significance: Deuteronomy 31:10–12 orders the Teaching read aloud every seventh year, at Sukkot, to men, women, children and strangers. Aaron Demsky compares the two.

events.description: Puduhepa, queen of Hittite king Hattusili III, orders the chief scribe to recopy older religious rituals, probably ones gathered long before from Kizzuwatna.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 31:24–26 has Moses write the Teaching “to the very end” and give the book to the Levites, to be kept beside the Ark.

events.description: Ramesses II's crown prince Khaemweset dies in his father's 55th year. His brother Merneptah, the 13th son, becomes crown prince and acts as regent for Ramesses' last twelve years.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 31:7 has Moses, still alive, charge Joshua “in the sight of all Israel” to lead the people into the land.

events.description: A Hittite treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa lists its witnesses: gods, then mountains, rivers and springs, “the great sea, heaven and earth, the winds, the clouds.”
events.significance: The song opens: “Give ear, O heavens, let me speak; Let the earth hear” (32:1). Shalom Holtz argues Moses' appeals to heaven and earth draw on such treaty witness lists.

events.description: In a treaty, Hittite king Tudhaliya IV names the kings who are “equal to me”: the kings of Egypt, of Babylon and of Assyria.
events.significance: The song pictures the world's map differently: “When the Most High gave nations their homes / And set the divisions of humankind” (32:8).

events.description: Tukulti-Ninurta I's victory over Babylon is told in a long Assyrian poem. It calls Babylon's king “the transgressor of an oath”, who so angered the gods that they left their shrines.
events.significance: Haazinu too explains disaster as the fruit of broken faith: Israel “forsook the God who made them” (32:15). Peter Machinist has compared the epic with the Bible.

events.description: Pharaoh Seti I, father of Ramesses II, dies. His tomb in the Valley of the Kings, KV17, is one of its largest, deepest and most decorated.
events.significance: Much later his mummy was moved to a royal cache. Of Moses, Deuteronomy 34:6 says “no one knows his burial place to this day.”

events.description: Hittite king Muwatalli II dies. His son Urhi-Teshub takes the throne as Mursili III, but seven years later his uncle Hattusili overthrows him.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 34:9: Joshua “was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands upon him; and the Israelites heeded him.”

events.description: Ramesses II dies at about 90, after a reign of 66 years. By then he suffered from arthritis, hardened arteries and severe dental problems.
events.significance: Deuteronomy 34:7: Moses was 120 when he died; “his eyes were undimmed and his vigor unabated.”
